specPoints.text: use the principle of conservation of energy

primer.text: Energy is the strictest accountant in physics: nothing created, nothing destroyed, everything transferred. This note states the principle, then walks it through a bat-and-ball strike, a boiling kettle and a trampoline cycle — watching useful and wasted branches close every account.

lessons.title: The principle of conservation of energy
sourceHeadings: What is the principle of conservation of energy?
Examples of the principle of conservation of energy
lessons.opening: One law underpins every energy account in physics: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores. A closed system keeps a constant total; whatever one system gains, another loses; and energy that spreads to the surroundings is never lost — merely no longer useful.
keyPoints: Energy is never created nor destroyed — it only moves between stores.
The total energy of a closed system remains constant.
Whatever one system gains, another system loses by the same amount.
Energy spreads out into the surroundings by heating and radiation — dissipated, and usually wasted.
Dissipated transfers are usually not useful, so the energy is described as wasted.

low.restatement: The books always balance: no transfer creates or destroys energy, closed systems keep their total, and the only place energy seems to vanish is into useless, dissipated spreading to the surroundings.
low.analogy: A sealed bag of marbles: you can pour them between pockets forever, but the bag’s count never changes.
low.examPointer: Use the exact statement in explain questions: cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another.

medium.restatement: Every gain is matched by an equal loss somewhere else; dissipation by heating and radiation spreads energy thinly through the surroundings, which is why it stops being useful without ever stopping to exist.
medium.analogy: A cup of tea cooling in a big cold room: the tea’s loss is the room’s gain, spread so thinly that no one can make a useful engine from it.
medium.examPointer: Wasted does not mean destroyed — say dissipated to the surroundings to keep the conservation law intact in your wording.

check.stem: Which statement is the principle of conservation of energy?

options.text: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores
options.explanation: This is the stated principle.

options.text: energy always decreases as it is used
options.explanation: Using energy transfers it; the total is constant.

options.text: energy is created usefully and destroyed wastefully
options.explanation: Neither creation nor destruction happens.

options.text: energy runs out when a machine stops
options.explanation: The energy has transferred to other stores, not ended.

check.stem: A closed system contains two objects that interact. If object A gains 30 J, what happens to object B?

options.text: B gains 30 J as well
options.explanation: That would create energy within the closed system.

options.text: B loses exactly 30 J
options.explanation: One system’s gain must equal the other’s loss inside a closed system.

options.text: B loses more than 30 J because of dissipation
options.explanation: Dissipation redistributes within the accounting; it does not inflate losses.

options.text: B is unaffected
options.explanation: The transfer came from somewhere.

check.stem: What does dissipated mean?

options.text: destroyed so it no longer exists
options.explanation: Dissipated energy still exists.

options.text: spread out to the surroundings, often by heating and radiation
options.explanation: Dissipation is spreading, usually by heating and radiation.

options.text: stored permanently in the thermal store
options.explanation: It is spread through the surroundings, not parked in one store.

options.text: converted back into chemical fuel
options.explanation: Nothing reverses like that in these scenarios.

check.stem: Why is dissipated energy often called wasted?

options.text: because it is destroyed
options.explanation: It is not destroyed; conservation forbids that.

options.text: because it has spread to the surroundings where it cannot be used for the intended purpose
options.explanation: Wasted energy is dissipated energy that no longer serves the purpose.

options.text: because it breaks the conservation law
options.explanation: Dissipation is fully compatible with conservation.

options.text: because it always leaves as sound
options.explanation: Heating is the more common dissipation route.

check.stem: A kettle boils water. Which transfer is the WASTED transfer?

options.text: mains supply to the heating element, electrically
options.explanation: That is the intended first link of the chain.

options.text: element to the water, by heating
options.explanation: Heating the water is the purpose of the kettle.

options.text: energy warming the plastic kettle body
options.explanation: The plastic body’s thermal store gain is not useful for boiling water.

options.text: water turning to steam
options.explanation: Boiling the water is exactly what the kettle is for.

check.stem: State what happens to the total energy of a closed system.
check.modelAnswer: The total energy of a closed system remains constant.

check.stem: State the two dissipation routes named in the principle’s description.
check.modelAnswer: Heating and radiation — the two dissipation routes named in the principle.

check.stem: Explain why a bouncing ball never quite returns to its release height, using the conservation law in your answer.
check.modelAnswer: At each bounce some energy is transferred out of the ball’s kinetic and elastic stores into the thermal stores of the ball and the floor, and some is radiated away as sound. The energy is not destroyed — the total is conserved — but the mechanical energy available for the rebound is reduced, so each bounce reaches a lower height.

check.stem: A trampoline jumper reaches the top of a bounce with 500 J in her gravitational store; at the top of the next bounce she has 420 J there. State the energy dissipated between the two tops and name one route it took.
check.modelAnswer: 500 - 420 = 80 J was dissipated between the two tops; one route is heating of the trampoline canvas and the air (with some sound radiated at the canvas).

lessons.title: Conservation in the bat-and-ball and kettle examples
sourceHeadings: Example 1: a bat hitting a ball
Example 2: Boiling Water in a Kettle
lessons.opening: Two everyday scenes carry the law through every store and pathway. A bat strikes a ball: kinetic energy splits into the ball’s motion, wasted thermal bumps and dissipated sound and heat. A kettle boils: electrical energy lands in the element, flows into the water, and leaks wastefully into the plastic and the air.
keyPoints: The moving bat holds energy in its kinetic store.
Some of the bat’s kinetic energy transfers usefully to the ball’s kinetic store.
Some transfers mechanically to the ball’s thermal store on impact, and some dissipates by heating to the bat, ball and surroundings — both wasted.
In the kettle, energy is transferred electrically from the mains to the element’s thermal store.
The element transfers energy by heating to the water (useful) and to the plastic kettle body and surroundings (wasted).

low.restatement: Bat-and-ball: kinetic store splits into useful kinetic of the ball plus wasted thermal and radiated sound. Kettle: electrical input lands in the element, flows by heating into the water, and the plastic and air take the wasted share.
low.analogy: A fruit tree shaken by a shake-and-catch harvester: some fruit lands in the basket (useful), some bruises on the ground (wasted) — but no fruit is created or destroyed.
low.examPointer: Name the pathway at each link: mechanically on impact, electrically from the mains, by heating into the water.

medium.restatement: Both examples close the same loop: the input store empties, useful and wasted branches fill, and the surroundings receive the dissipated remainder — every joule accounted for.
medium.analogy: Splitting a pizza: the slices go to guests (useful), crumbs to the floor (wasted), but the pizza’s total never changes.
medium.examPointer: Questions often ask for ONE wasted transfer — the plastic kettle body and the sound of the strike are the classic answers.

check.stem: In the bat-and-ball impact, which transfer is USEFUL?

options.text: bat kinetic store to ball kinetic store
options.explanation: Sending the ball on its way is the purpose of the strike.

options.text: bat kinetic store to ball thermal store
options.explanation: Warming the ball is not the aim.

options.text: bat kinetic store to surroundings by sound
options.explanation: The crack of the bat is dissipated sound.

options.text: ball thermal store to bat thermal store
options.explanation: No useful purpose is served by heating either way.

check.stem: How is energy transferred from the bat’s kinetic store to the ball’s thermal store?

options.text: mechanically, due to the impact
options.explanation: The impact’s mechanical work deforms and warms the ball.

options.text: electrically
options.explanation: No circuit is involved.

options.text: by radiation only
options.explanation: Radiation is the sound route, not the impact route.

options.text: by convection
options.explanation: Convection needs a fluid current; the impact is a solid contact.

check.stem: In the kettle, what is the FIRST store to receive the energy from the mains?

options.text: the water’s thermal store
options.explanation: The element warms first; the water receives energy from the element.

options.text: the heating element’s thermal store
options.explanation: Energy is transferred electrically to the element’s thermal store.

options.text: the plastic kettle’s thermal store
options.explanation: The plastic receives wasted energy later.

options.text: the surroundings
options.explanation: Dissipation comes last.

check.stem: Which kettle transfer is wasted?

options.text: element to water by heating
options.explanation: That is the kettle’s job.

options.text: mains to element electrically
options.explanation: The intended input link.

options.text: element to plastic kettle body by heating
options.explanation: Warming the plastic serves no purpose.

options.text: water to steam at boiling point
options.explanation: Boiling is the desired outcome.

check.stem: The bat’s kinetic store loses 200 J in the strike. Which set of destinations could conserve energy?

options.text: 120 J to the ball’s kinetic store, 50 J to thermal stores, 30 J radiated as sound: 200 J total
options.explanation: The shares sum to exactly 200 J, so the books balance.

options.text: 120 J to the ball’s kinetic store and 50 J to thermal stores: 170 J total
options.explanation: 30 J has vanished, which conservation forbids.

options.text: 220 J to the ball’s kinetic store alone
options.explanation: More energy arrives than left the bat.

options.text: 200 J destroyed by friction
options.explanation: Friction transfers; it does not destroy.

check.stem: State the pathway for each link: (a) mains to kettle element, (b) element to water.
check.modelAnswer: (a) electrical work from the mains supply; (b) heating from the element to the water.

check.stem: In the bat-and-ball example, state the two stores that receive WASTED energy.
check.modelAnswer: Thermal stores — of the ball, the bat and the surroundings — receive wasted energy (with some dissipated by heating and radiated as sound).

check.stem: Explain why the bat, the ball and the air all end up very slightly warmer after the strike.
check.modelAnswer: The strike cannot transfer all of the bat’s kinetic energy into the ball’s motion: impact deformation transfers energy mechanically into thermal stores, and heating and radiation dissipate more into the surroundings. Since energy is conserved rather than destroyed, those spreads show up as tiny temperature rises everywhere the wasted energy landed.

check.stem: A kettle element receives 180 kJ from the mains. 150 kJ ends up in the water and steam. Name the account that holds the difference and state its size.
check.modelAnswer: The missing 30 kJ sits in wasted transfers — the plastic kettle’s thermal store and the dissipated surroundings — because conservation requires the full 180 kJ to be accounted for.

lessons.title: Conservation on the trampoline
lessons.opening: A trampoline bounces the conservation law through four stores in one motion: gravitational store empties into kinetic on the way down, kinetic fills the elastic store as the canvas stretches, and the sequence reverses on the way up — shrinking a little each bounce as heating and sound take their share.
keyPoints: Falling: the jumper’s gravitational store transfers to the kinetic store.
At the canvas: kinetic transfers to the elastic store as the canvas stretches.
Rebounding: the elastic store returns energy to kinetic, then to gravitational as the jumper rises.
Each cycle transfers some energy to thermal stores and to sound, so the bounces shrink.
The jumper must supply fresh energy mechanically to keep bouncing at the same height.

low.restatement: The trampoline cycle is gravitational → kinetic → elastic → kinetic → gravitational, with thermal and sound skimming a little off every pass — the shrinking bounce is conservation made visible.
low.analogy: Water sloshing between four buckets through a leaky pipe: the water shuttles forever, but a few drops spill on every trip.
low.examPointer: Order the stores correctly for the phase asked: descending is gravitational to kinetic; stretched canvas is elastic.

medium.restatement: At every exchange some energy takes the heating or sound exit, so the maximum height falls unless the jumper’s muscles do mechanical work to refill the account.
medium.analogy: A payment where every transfer charges a small fee: the balance still exists but the useful balance shrinks each round trip.
medium.examPointer: If asked why the jumper keeps bouncing lower, name BOTH wasted routes: heating of the canvas and body, and sound.

check.stem: As the jumper falls towards the canvas, which transfer occurs?

options.text: kinetic store to gravitational store
options.explanation: That is the rising phase.

options.text: gravitational store to kinetic store
options.explanation: Falling empties the gravitational store into the kinetic store.

options.text: elastic store to kinetic store
options.explanation: The canvas is not yet stretched.

options.text: thermal store to kinetic store
options.explanation: The thermal store is where wasted energy ends up, not the source here.

check.stem: At the lowest point of the bounce, which store holds most of the energy?

options.text: the gravitational store
options.explanation: The jumper is at minimum height there.

options.text: the kinetic store
options.explanation: The jumper is momentarily at rest at the lowest point.

options.text: the elastic store of the stretched canvas
options.explanation: Maximum stretch means maximum elastic energy.

options.text: the chemical store
options.explanation: Chemical energy is the jumper’s internal fuel, not the bounce account.

check.stem: Why do the bounces get lower each time?

options.text: energy is destroyed at each bounce
options.explanation: Nothing is destroyed; it is dissipated.

options.text: some energy is dissipated by heating and radiated as sound each cycle
options.explanation: The wasted transfers shrink the mechanical account each round trip.

options.text: gravity gets stronger near the canvas
options.explanation: Gravity is essentially constant over the bounce height.

options.text: the canvas loses its elasticity permanently
options.explanation: The canvas rebounds fine; the losses are thermal and sound.

check.stem: Which pathway delivers fresh energy when the jumper jumps higher from the canvas?

options.text: electrically
options.explanation: No circuit is involved.

options.text: by radiation
options.explanation: Radiation is an output here, not an input.

options.text: mechanically, from the jumper’s muscles pushing on the canvas
options.explanation: Muscles do mechanical work to refill the bounce account.

options.text: by heating from the sun
options.explanation: Sunbathing does not power the bounce.

check.stem: Between two successive tops, the gravitational store holds 500 J then 420 J. The missing 80 J is:

options.text: destroyed during the bounce
options.explanation: Conservation forbids destruction.

options.text: dissipated to thermal stores and radiated as sound
options.explanation: The difference is exactly the wasted share of the cycle.

options.text: still in the elastic store at the top
options.explanation: At the top the canvas is unstretched.

options.text: impossible to know without measuring sound
options.explanation: Conservation pins the total; the split between routes is the only detail.

check.stem: State the order of stores in one full trampoline cycle, starting from the top of a bounce.
check.modelAnswer: Gravitational, then kinetic, then elastic, then kinetic, then gravitational again — with thermal and sound taking wasted shares at each exchange.

check.stem: State the pathway by which the jumper’s muscles add energy at each bounce.
check.modelAnswer: Mechanically — the muscles do mechanical work pushing against the canvas.

check.stem: Explain why the jumper’s body and the trampoline canvas are slightly warmer after a session of bouncing.
check.modelAnswer: Every stretch of the canvas and every impact dissipates some energy by heating into the canvas and the jumper’s body, and some radiates away as sound. The energy is conserved, but the repeated wasted transfers accumulate as small temperature rises in the materials involved.

check.stem: A jumper’s first top-of-bounce gravitational store holds 600 J and each cycle wastes 12% of the mechanical energy. State the gravitational-store energy at the third top of bounce.
check.modelAnswer: Cycle 1: 600 × 0.88 = 528 J; cycle 2: 528 × 0.88 = about 465 J at the third top.

glossary.definition: The principle that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another.
A system that exchanges no energy with its surroundings, so its total energy stays constant.
Spread out to the surroundings, usually by heating and radiation, so the energy is no longer useful.
Energy transferred to stores that do not serve the intended purpose.
The energy store of stretched, squashed or bent objects.
